_about: Flame Atlas prepared answers (Team Flame Atlas, NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026). Answers to the questions the dashboard's buttons ask, written in advance with an AI assistant (Claude) from the team's curated NASA documents and tests table, and checked against the cited source pages in a second AI pass; same format as the live chat's answers. Every point names its source and page.

answers.question: What do the papers add for Epoxy/glass at 30% O2, 70.3 kPa?

data.heading: How far to trust the dots
data.text: Every Epoxy/glass oxygen threshold in the documents comes from one parametric-effects paper on a 0.064-inch NEMA G-11 laminate: 1-g upward tests at 101.3 kPa in initially quiescent gas, oxygen stepped 1% at a time, with no igniter stated for these results.

data.heading: A coated fiberglass-epoxy cover
data.text: A 2026 report on reduced-pressure atmospheres, in a qualitative review with limited materials information, calls a Dapco 2030-coated fiberglass-epoxy acoustic cover nonflammable at 30% O2 and 70.3 kPa but likely flammable at 34 to 40% O2 and 56.5 kPa.

data.heading: Watch out
data.text: For the 0.064-inch Epoxy/glass laminate in 1-g upward threshold tests at 101.3 kPa in initially quiescent gas, half-inch-wide strips without side support gave a ULOI of 17.9% O2, standard-mounted 2.5-inch-wide samples 23.6%, a reduction the authors call significant.

inferred.text: 30% O2 is about 6 points above the highest Epoxy/glass threshold and 70.3 kPa about 31 kPa below their pressure; no Epoxy/glass threshold at reduced pressure or in low gravity is documented.

answers.question: What do the papers add for ETFE wire insulation at 30% O2, 70.3 kPa?

data.heading: How far to trust the dots
data.text: The wire study prints no pressure, and its microgravity runs were parabolic flights of 0.01 g at 5 to 20 cm/s opposed flow. Its limits tended to fall as flow fell; the authors say confirming a quenching branch needs forced flows below 5 cm/s.

data.heading: Two other studies agree
data.text: The wire study reports that two other studies, by Osorio and by Mizutani, also measured ETFE-insulated copper wire in normal gravity and microgravity and reported a significant drop in limiting oxygen concentration in microgravity.

data.heading: Watch out
data.text: ETFE on a nickel-chrome core spread steadily in parabolic-flight microgravity at 23% O2 in 5 cm/s opposed flow; the authors say that, since the core changes how the insulation burns, a wire should be rated as a whole, not by its insulation alone.

inferred.text: 30% O2 is about 2 points above the lowest oxygen where copper-core ETFE wire spread in microgravity at 5 and 12 cm/s opposed flow, read from a figure, and below every 1-g limit; pressure unprinted.

answers.question: What do the papers add for Ethylene-nitrogen gas (burner) at 30% O2, 70.3 kPa?

data.heading: How far to trust the dots
data.text: Each test is a gas flame on a 25 or 50 mm porous burner aboard the ISS, emulating real solid and liquid fuels. A test recorded as burned was still alight when the fuel was shut off on purpose, after 64.5 to 300 s.

data.heading: The PSI record on elevated oxygen
data.text: The experiment's PSI record, which calls its results still preliminary, reports that ongoing burning without air flow in microgravity was seen notably in elevated-oxygen atmospheres considered for future spacecraft, whereas such flames in a normal 21% oxygen atmosphere self-extinguished in a short time.

data.heading: Watch out
data.text: At nominal 26.5% O2 and 70 kPa on the 25 mm burner, the same fuel mixture gave flames that lasted to fuel shut-off and flames that self-extinguished, for undiluted ethylene and for two nitrogen dilutions.

inferred.text: 70.3 kPa matches the thesis's habitat pressure of 70 kPa, but 30% O2 is above the nominal 26.5% tested there; at 70 to 75 kPa no test went above about 29% O2.

answers.question: What do the papers add for Japan wax at 30% O2, 70.3 kPa?

data.heading: How far to trust the dots
data.text: Japan wax was tested only as candles in the ISS glovebox, which an ISS combustion guide says is normally limited to ISS air, nominally 21% O2 and about 101 kPa; recorded values span 15.9 to 21.24% O2 and, where logged, 98.3 to 99.5 kPa.

data.heading: BASS runs at 21.24% O2
data.text: In the BASS runs of 16 August 2012 on the ISS, logged at 21.24% O2 and 98.5 kPa, each Japan wax candle flame went out at fan potentiometer settings 0.31 or 0.32, when the flow was cut to zero, or when the wax ran out.

data.heading: Watch out
data.text: In the BASS-II Japan wax candle burn on the ISS at calibrated 17.4% O2, the wick ejected a wax droplet upstream at potentiometer 0.4; the authors say that in microgravity, with low enough melt viscosity, burning droplets can be ejected and possibly ignite other materials.

inferred.text: At 30% O2 and 70.3 kPa, oxygen is over 8.5 points above every Japan wax test and pressure about 28 kPa or more below every logged one; whether the low-flow extinctions hold there is open.

With no airflow in microgravity, the paper gives diameters of average mass 30 to 40% larger than in flow tests for all materials and, in its conclusions, particles 2 to 3 times larger than at 8 cm/s.

sources.locator: 4. Impact of flow on particle morphology

data.text: Three instruments measured number, diameter and mass concentration; the geometric mean diameter, unlike the count mean and diameter of average mass, assumes a log-normal distribution the paper says its data cannot test directly, though two indications support it.
In baseline runs (ISS; 8 cm/s airflow; sample temperature chosen for 1 to 2 mg weight loss in 60 s), the unaged diameter of average mass ranged from 0.101 µm for Kapton to 0.465 µm for silicone.

The zero-flow condition, added by changing the valve operation, was run in 11 tests; in them about half the smoke was lost by diffusing out of the inlet into the glovebox volume, so total particle counts were lower than normal and the TEM grids held few particles.

sources.locator: 4. Impact of flow on particle morphology
4. Impact of flow on particle morphology

data.text: A prototype two-moment sensor (MPASS) flown on the reflight was correlated by least squares on all test points with a signal-to-noise ratio above 2, whatever the material, heating rate or ageing time; the paper says this cut the relative variance of its response by roughly a factor of at least 2 against a conventional single-output sensor.
The SAME-R record says its flight tests ran on the ISS from July 16 to September 9, 2010 and completed 66 test points.

inferred.text: SAME-R heated samples below their ignition point to study the smoke they give off, so its results bear on detecting a fire by its smoke, not on whether a material ignites or spreads flame at a given oxygen and pressure.

The 200 to 400 nm summary names no diameter measure, and in the baseline table at most four of the ten values of each diameter fall in that range, so the summary cannot be read as each material's baseline size.

other_side.note: zero-flow runs gave larger particles than flow runs, against most average sizes at 200 to 400 nm

lead.text: SAME-R's ISS smoke from materials heated below ignition had average particle sizes mostly 200 to 400 nm, some no-airflow cases substantially larger; the reflight paper gives no 1-g smoke sizes.

answer.not_covered: The documents give no oxygen, pressure or sample temperature for SAME-R.

answers.question: What did SAME find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: The 2012 reflight paper says SAME flew twice, in 2007 (SAME-1) and 2010 (SAME-2), and presents results from the 2010 reflight, the flight of the SAME-R record (July 16 to September 9, 2010).

The electron-microscope (TEM) grids from SAME-1 came back contaminated with extraneous particles, whose origin the reflight paper says was still under investigation; the SAME-R record calls all of SAME's grids unusable, although some showed shapes of certain smoke particles.

The reflight paper cites a 2008 paper on smoke particle size in low gravity, listed in the SAME record, for DustTrak results in which substantial portions of the lamp-wick and silicone particle distributions had aerodynamic diameters above 1 µm; it names neither flight nor conditions.

A 2020 fire-safety plan says a space experiment on smoke from several spacecraft materials found that typical smoke particle sizes can range from 100 to 500 nm in diameter of average mass, citing a 2018 paper that both SAME and SAME-R records list; the plan names neither the experiment nor the flight.

sources.locator: C. Fire Detection: Validation and Vehicle Scale Transport

data.text: The SAME record states objectives, not results: to measure the sizes that liquid smoke particles reach in low gravity, relate them to how the smoke was generated and carried, and develop a code predicting smoke droplet growth.

The record's approach: on the ISS, smoke came from overheated spacecraft materials in the Glovebox; an igniter was switched on for a preset 15 to 60 s, each event typically lasted 2 minutes, and thermophoretic samplers collected particles for electron-microscope sizing after flight.
A 2016 Saffire status paper says SAME investigated the size of smoke particles produced in low gravity, and that smoke transport models developed from these results have not been validated.

inferred.text: The SAME record's dates, March 2001 to February 2008, take in the 2007 flight and end before the 2010 reflight, which has its own record (SAME-R), so the reflight measurements the paper reports belong to SAME-R, not to this record.

The cited DustTrak result was published in 2008, before the reflight, and only SAME-1 carried two DustTraks, with 1 µm and 10 µm inlet impactors, to measure the share of particles above 1 µm; so it likely comes from the first flight, though the reflight paper does not say so.
SAME's smoke came from overheated spacecraft materials, so its data would bear on detecting a fire by its smoke, not on whether a material ignites or spreads flame at a given oxygen and pressure.

other_side.note: no result the documents tie to the first flight, so no evidence either way

lead.text: The documents hold no numerical smoke-particle sizes or smoke-detector readings from SAME's first flight in 2007.

answer.not_covered: The documents give no oxygen, pressure or sample temperature for any SAME run.

answers.question: What did SLICE find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: The SLICE record (PSI-106) states objectives, not results: the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity, including liftoff velocity limits for different fuels and burner diameters and how nitrogen fuel dilution affects soot formation and flame stability.

The record describes flames of fuels such as methane, ethylene and nitrogen-diluted mixtures, lit manually in controlled coflow air in a fan-driven duct with exchangeable burner tubes; more than 4,000 high-resolution images were captured across 13 testing experiments.
The record lists five published papers and one experimental table file; their results are not in these documents.

The 2015 ISS combustion researcher's guide says SLICE uses the SPICE hardware in the station glovebox and started and completed its operations in 2012; exploratory SLICE tests on lifted flames ran on the ISS in 2009 as part of SPICE.

The record's hypothesis, not a reported result, is that in microgravity the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames are significantly influenced by burner diameter, coflow velocity and fuel composition, and are fundamentally different from flames on Earth.

inferred.text: SLICE burned gaseous fuels from burner tubes in coflow air, so its planned liftoff limits would describe when such a flame detaches from the burner, not how a solid cabin material ignites or spreads flame.

other_side.note: no measured SLICE results in the documents, so no evidence either way

lead.text: The documents hold no measured SLICE results: no liftoff limits, flame lengths, soot or radiative heat-loss values.

answer.not_covered: The documents give no oxygen, pressure or coflow speed for any SLICE flame.

answers.question: What did SPICE find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: The SPICE record (PSI-107) states objectives, not results: laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames in coflow in microgravity, how burner diameter and coflow velocity affect luminous flame length and smoke point, and the sooting propensity of fuels.

The record describes an ISS glovebox apparatus burning fuels including methane, ethylene, propane, propylene and propylene mixtures with burner diameters of 0.41, 0.76 and 1.6 mm and 5.4 to 65 cm/s coflow, fuel flow adjusted to find the smoke point; it counts 526 flames studied.
The record lists nine publications, three with smoke points in their titles, and data files including 172 raw-data files and three reports; their results are not in these documents.

The 2015 ISS combustion researcher's guide says SPICE was conducted in 2009 in the ISS glovebox and investigated the transition from non-sooting to sooting; a photo in it shows SPICE flames going from non-smoking to a fully open, smoking flame tip as fuel flow increases.
A BASS slide deck says BASS used the on-orbit SPICE hardware, with minor modifications made to burn solid samples.

inferred.text: SPICE burned gaseous fuels from burners of 0.41 to 1.6 mm, so its smoke points describe when gas-jet flames start emitting soot, not how solid cabin materials ignite or spread flame.

other_side.note: no measured SPICE results in the documents, so no evidence either way

lead.text: The documents hold no measured SPICE results: no smoke points, luminous flame lengths or radiative heat-loss values.

answer.not_covered: No document gives the oxygen or pressure of the SPICE flames.

answers.question: What did Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: The PSI-115 record describes a ground study, January 2017 to December 2019, that set out to use numerical simulation to quantify how microgravity smoke differs from Earth-gravity smoke and which fluid-dynamic mechanisms cause the differences.

The record's approach is direct numerical simulation of dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) particle formation and growth in Earth gravity and microgravity from the pyrolysis vapor of a heated sample, in a geometry similar to SAME's, at two cross-flow speeds low enough that buoyancy matters under gravity.

The record says the simulations assess how particle size distributions depend on thermophoresis, particle settling and flow geometry, and that buoyancy-driven differences in wake geometry were examined at the lower of the two flow speeds; no outcome is given.
The record lists no publications and no experimental table; its files are 44 analysed-data files, one report, one science document and one metadata file, none of them among these documents.

The record's hypothesis, not a finding: without buoyancy, mixing and heat transfer are reduced and the time-temperature history of the vapors and the particle trajectories change significantly, changing the composition of the smoke.

inferred.text: The record's title says it uses SAME data, but its approach describes only simulations in a SAME-like geometry, with no stated comparison against SAME measurements, so any prediction it holds is a model result whose check against flight data the documents do not show.

other_side.note: no results in the documents, so no evidence either way

lead.text: The documents hold no results of PSI-115, such as simulated smoke particle sizes for microgravity and Earth gravity.

answer.not_covered: The documents give no cross-flow speed or sample temperature for the simulations.

answers.question: What did Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: The PSI-117 record describes a ground study, February 2017 to February 2022, that set out to use FLEX flight data from PSI to quantify how imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulated the dynamics and fate of established droplet cool flames.

Its approach is a 3-D OpenFOAM model of n-alkane droplet cool flames in microgravity, whose fidelity the record says was established against ISS FLEX measurements, run on 1 to 4 mm and about 0.5 mm droplets to build stability maps.
The record lists ten published papers and 15 files: ten analysed-data files, four presentations and a dissertation; neither the papers nor the files are among these documents.

The record's hypothesis, not a reported result: external thermo-convective perturbations, such as imposed temperature gradients, non-uniform heating or oscillatory or shear inflow, would govern cool-flame ignition, oscillation, transition to hot ignition and extinction by shifting residence time and scalar dissipation, and would dominate transport in microgravity, where buoyancy is suppressed.

The record states its space benefit as potential to improve spacecraft fire-safety modelling by resolving cool-flame and extinction behaviour in microgravity, using FLEX to define safer operating envelopes and materials; it gives no such envelope.

inferred.text: Any stability map from this study would be a CFD prediction checked against FLEX droplet flights, not a new flight test, and no document shows how closely the model matched those flights.

other_side.note: no results of this study in the documents, so no evidence either way

lead.text: The documents hold no results of the PSI-117 droplet cool-flame simulations: no stability maps, ignition delays, oscillation frequencies or extinction diameters.

answer.not_covered: No solid fuel or spacecraft material is part of this study.

data.text: The PSI-142 record reports that the warm flame has a double reaction-zone structure and plays a critical role in the transition between cool and hot flames; it gives no fuel, oxygen or pressure for this result.

The record also reports that at elevated pressures the flammable region of warm and cool flames expands, which it attributes to low- and intermediate-temperature reactivity rising with pressure; no pressure value comes with this result.

Its approach compared oxygen effects on cool-flame extinction limits at FLEX flight conditions with three numerical schemes: n-heptane/air spark-assisted propagation, one-dimensional dimethyl ether flames, and dimethyl ether/air cool-flame regimes and burning limits at up to about 2,030 kPa.

The record describes a ground study, August 2016 to July 2021, on principal-investigator laboratory hardware, that set out to use FLEX data for new simulations and ground experiments with ozone-sensitized counterflow flames, among them a new flammability-limit diagram for diffusional cool flames.

The record lists 12 publications, all marked published, and two data files, an analysed-data workbook and an experimental summary table; neither the publications nor the files are among these documents.

inferred.text: With no values given, neither reported result can be set against any test in these documents, or checked for the oxygen and pressure range it covers.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

answers.question: What did ACME CFI-G find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: The PSI record states objectives, not results: in ISS tests, the conditions under which cool diffusion flames, whose peak temperatures it puts at 500 to 1000 K, occur for propane, n-butane and n-pentane, in normal and inverse flames.

The record's hypotheses for the ISS tests, not results, include steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners, and cool flames that extinguish when the flow rate drops and become hot diffusion flames when it rises.

The record's approach is spherical diffusion flame tests aboard the ISS with several fuels and a range of reactant dilutions, flow rates and pressures, for normal and inverse convection directions, observed with cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes and thermocouples.
The record leaves the investigation dates blank and lists two publications, two experimental tables, for normal and inverse flames, and 3749 raw data files.
The record's stated impact is that its measurements will help test and advance cool-flame kinetics mechanisms, which should facilitate more efficient internal combustion engines.

inferred.text: Propane, n-butane and n-pentane fed through a porous burner are gas flames, so any cool-flame limits in the record's publications and data files, which the documents do not include, would not describe how a solid cabin material burns.

other_side.note: no results in the documents, so no evidence either way

lead.text: The documents hold no results of ACME CFI-G, such as measured conditions for cool diffusion flames or their extinction.

answer.not_covered: The documents give no oxygen or pressure value for any ACME CFI-G test.

answers.question: What did ACME BRE find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: ACME BRE burned no material sample: ethylene-nitrogen or methane-nitrogen gas flowed through a porous burner to emulate real solid and liquid fuels, which the thesis matches to its flames by heat of combustion and heat of gasification.

On the ISS in still air, some ethylene-nitrogen flames on the 25 mm burner burned until the fuel was shut off on purpose, at nominal 40% O2 and 1 bar, 34% O2 at 1 and 0.56 bar, and 26.5% O2 at 0.7 bar.
On the ISS, every ethylene-nitrogen flame lit at nominal 21% or 25% O2, all at 1 bar, self-extinguished within 90 seconds.

In ISS tests at nominal 34% O2 and 0.56 bar with undiluted ethylene, flames at fuel mass fluxes of 1.78 and 2.55 g/m2s reached steady state, as the thesis describes them, before an intentional shutdown at about 3 minutes; the flame at 6.95 g/m2s self-extinguished. For these undiluted flames, the thesis places the self-extinguished ones above 3 g/m2s.
In ISS tests with methane-nitrogen on the 25 mm burner at 1.03 to 1.06 bar, every flame self-extinguished within 45 seconds, including tests at 39 to 40% O2.

All the thesis's experiments were transient; it judges the ISS flames on the 25 mm burner that burned to fuel shut-off close to steady from its analytical solution. That solution puts their size on average at 94% of the steady value in the Chapter 6 summary and their height at 95.3% in the steadiness analysis, standard deviation 1.9%.

sources.locator: 6.4 An analysis of the steadiness of flames
5.1 Analysis of the steadiness of the flame heights

data.text: The PSI record calls BRE's results still preliminary, while saying they suggest NASA may want to increase use of its alternative flammability Test 2, with the cone calorimeter, which can measure material properties corresponding to the microgravity flames observed with the BRE burner.

The thesis prints different pressures for some first-round tests in its two test tables: test 51A1 at 1.02 bar in Table 3.1, and test 19051A1, whose mass flux, heat fluxes and flame size match, at 0.565 bar in Table 6.1; the text and the Figure 3.3 caption put 51A1 at 1 bar.

inferred.text: Every test ran in still air on a 25 or 50 mm burner, so the results describe a small burning surface with no air flow, the condition the PSI record links to shutting off ventilation to put out spacecraft fires, rather than a fire spreading in cabin airflow.

other_side.note: every flame at nominal 21 or 25% O2 and 1 bar went out, against flames that burned to fuel shut-off at nominal 34 to 40% O2, and 26.5% at 0.7 bar

lead.text: On the ISS in still air, some ethylene-nitrogen burner flames lasted to fuel shut-off at nominal 34–40% O2 and 1 bar, none at nominal 21–25%; no material sample burned.

answer.not_covered: The documents give no heat of gasification, a property the emulation matches, for Nomex, Kapton or PTFE.

answers.question: What did ACME CLD Flame find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: The PSI record states objectives, not results: data to test computational models at the extremes of fuel dilution, from flame shape, lift-off height, temperatures, extinction limits and soot of methane and ethylene coflow diffusion flames, as functions of velocity and fuel dilution.

The record plans OH* and CH* chemiluminescence for lift-off height and flame shape of the more dilute flames as extinction is approached, soot luminosity and laser extinction for soot temperature and volume fraction of the more fuel-rich flames, and thin-filament pyrometry for flame temperature in non-sooting regions; the kinetics and soot models can then be adjusted to match.
The record's stated impacts include that understanding the factors that affect flame extinction in diffusion flames is critical in the suppression of fires and in improving engine efficiency.
The record lists the ISS as platform with ACME and Combustion Integrated Rack hardware, dates the investigation October 2006 to May 2022, and lists 18 publication entries and one experimental table.

A 2015 researcher's guide to ISS combustion science lists CLD Flame among five planned ACME experiments and says that, unlike the others, the Burning Rate Emulator is focused on fire prevention, especially in spacecraft.

inferred.text: These are methane and ethylene gas flames in an air coflow, so any extinction limits in the record's publications and data table, which the documents do not include, would describe gas flames rather than a solid cabin material.

other_side.note: no results in the documents, so no evidence either way

lead.text: The documents hold no results of ACME CLD Flame, such as a measured lift-off height, extinction limit or soot volume fraction.

answer.not_covered: The documents give no oxygen, pressure or flow value for any ACME CLD Flame test.

answers.question: What did ACME E-FIELD Flames find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: The PSI record reports, without values, that voltage-current curves revealed ion-driven convection effects, in ISS tests of nitrogen-diluted methane and ethylene flames with up to 10 kV applied between the burner and a mesh above it.

The record says nitrogen dilution was varied from highly stable to near-extinction flames, along with fuel flow rate, coflow velocity and field polarity, on a gas-jet burner and on the CLD Flame coflow burner.

The record lists high-resolution cameras for flame shape, luminosity and soot distribution, filtered spectral imaging for chemiluminescent emission and soot volume fraction, and thermopile detectors for flame radiant emission, with Glenn Research Center directing the astronauts' actions.

The record says the research is not being conducted to serve any space application, though it is possible its findings could aid future space-based combustion devices, for example for solid waste processing.
The record dates the investigation November 2016 to November 2020 and lists 25 publications and one experimental table.

inferred.text: These are nitrogen-diluted gas flames under an applied voltage, so even the record's one qualitative finding concerns controlled burner flames, not how a solid cabin material ignites or spreads flame.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence: the record gives one qualitative finding and no test values

lead.text: For ACME E-FIELD Flames, the PSI record states that voltage-current curves from ISS tests revealed ion-driven convection effects, but reports no measured value.

answer.not_covered: The documents give no oxygen or pressure value for any ACME E-FIELD Flames test.

answers.question: What did ACME s-Flame find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: The PSI record states objectives, not results: the transient structure and quasi-steady extinction limits of spherical diffusion flames of soot-free hydrogen-methane-diluent and sooty ethylene-diluent mixtures, and the onset of predicted pulsating instabilities, for comparison with detailed simulations.

The record says little of the planned test matrix can be adequately explored in ground facilities because of time and g-jitter limits, and that the flight experiment definition will rely on the modelling, also used to develop its test conditions.

The record proposes fuels including hydrogen, methane and ethylene, mixed with nitrogen, helium or carbon dioxide, issuing from a spherical porous burner into an oxidizing environment, with synchronized spectrally resolved images, flame and burner temperatures, radiative flux, flow rates, ambient temperatures, pressures and acceleration levels.
The record dates the investigation February 2015 to November 2019 and lists 44 publications, 4058 raw data files and 50 reference data files.

A 2015 researcher's guide to ISS combustion science lists s-Flame among five planned ACME experiments and says that, unlike the others, the Burning Rate Emulator is focused on fire prevention, especially in spacecraft.

inferred.text: Any extinction limits in the record's data files would describe gas mixtures on a spherical porous burner, with test conditions developed from the model, rather than a solid cabin material.

other_side.note: no results in the documents, so no evidence either way

answers.question: What did BASS-II find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: For cast PMMA rods in concurrent flow on the ISS, the flammability boundary reaches its minimum, about 13.5% final O2, at a stretch rate of 8 to 12 s⁻¹, below a cited 15.4% O2 limit for 1-g upward spread with 4 cm/s added flow.

For black cast PMMA rods in opposed flow on the ISS at low forced flow, the chapter gives spread at O2 as low as 17.5% in its text and at about 16.8% on 6.35-mm rods in its spread-rate plot (read from a figure), against none below 19% O2 in 1-g ground tests without radiant heating.
Three Nomex III samples on the ISS, in concurrent flow of 8 to 15 cm/s at 21 to 22.2% initial O2, gave no sustained flame; the test table records at most brief ignition.

sources.locator: Columns in test matrix: Air display

data.text: For the cotton-fiberglass SIBAL fabric, about 0.32 mm thick and 1.2 or 2.2 cm wide, in concurrent flow on the ISS at 1 atm and 16.9 to 18.7% O2, the six quenching tests went out when the flow was lowered to between 1 and 5 cm/s, the quenching flow being higher at lower O2.

For the concurrent PMMA rods tested on the ISS, ignited generally at 5 cm/s, the time to a sustained flame reached 230 s, longest for larger rods at lower O2. The authors write that the 25 s ignition time of the NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 may be too short for a flammability test and so may make it an ignition test.

BASS-II ran 126 tests on the ISS, more than the 103 planned, because some samples were burned more than once; the film and rod tasks also changed the flow during a burn to get several test conditions from one sample.

Test oxygen comes from sensor readings taken before and after each test, with 0.1% O2 resolution and a daily offset against the station's Major Constituents Analyzer, as the sensor is not recalibrated on orbit.
Fan voltage was calibrated daily against an airspeed probe with about 1 min response and ±0.5 cm/s effective resolution; the report notes high error bars at flows around 1 cm/s and below.

inferred.text: Both PMMA rod gaps compare weak forced flow in microgravity with the much stronger buoyant flow of the 1-g tests, so they show what the low-flow regime adds rather than a gravity effect at equal flow.

The Nomex III result rests on three concurrent-flow samples at 21 to 22.2% O2, so it shows no sustained flame at those settings but not where a Nomex III limit would lie at lower flow or other oxygen levels.

other_side.note: Nomex III gave no sustained flame, against PMMA rods that burned below the 1-g limits the report compares them with

lead.text: On ISS, PMMA rods in weak flow burned below 1-g oxygen limits the report compares them with; Nomex III samples sustained no flame; lowest-flow calibration has high error bars.

answer.not_covered: No BASS-II test above 22.2% O2 or at reduced pressure.

answers.question: What did BASS find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: Cotton-fiberglass fabric on ISS spread steadily against 10 cm/s opposed flow until the fuel ran out (O2 not stated); in 1 g it cannot spread downward in normal air, and the authors call this enhanced flammability in microgravity for this geometry.

sources.locator: Comparison of 0-g and 1-g Opposed Flow Flames

data.text: The BASS deck reports Ultem and Nomex HT90-40 did not burn on ISS at 21–22% O2 and about 15 cm/s, similar to 1 g but on narrower samples; logged 'Nomex blend' runs at 21.6% and 22.5% O2 ignited briefly, one only with the igniter on.

On ISS at 22% O2, 1 atm and 14 to 15 cm/s concurrent flow, a 2-cm-wide Nomex-III sample burned with the igniter left on until the flame spread away, then narrowed and went out within 1 cm of the sample end; the deck notes 22% O2 is its 1-g ULOI, on a narrower sample here.

On ISS at 17% O2 in nitrogen, 1 atm and below 1 cm/s, a nitrogen jet near the end of a burn of PMMA of 15-mm initial diameter failed to extinguish the flame. The authors attribute this, for the given flow rate, to thicker solids that can store a great deal of heat even with only a small flame.

The ISS as-run log records nitrogen putting out flames on two 2-cm spheres: PMMA at 22.6% O2, 102.2 kPa and air display 5, and, eventually, one at 22.4% O2 and 100.1 kPa turned down to a minimum flame. One run later, at the same O2, pressure and air display, nitrogen blew out only part of the first sphere's flame.
BASS made 115 burns of 41 samples on ISS: 17 thin flat, 12 spheres, 4 thick flat, 8 candles; airflow speed was the main variable.

The as-run log gives one O2 and one pressure value for each of its 121 test rows, under the heading 'ISS environment', spanning 15.9% to 22.7% O2 and 98.3 to 102.2 kPa. For as-run tests 86 and 87 the notes give 17.3% and 16.8% O2 after nitrogen dilution, while the O2 column reads 21.1%.

as run matrix, rows 4 to 129, columns AA and AB

inferred.text: Ultem and Nomex HT90-40 were run below the 23.5% O2 ULOI the deck lists for both, so the lack of a sustained flame on ISS leaves open whether their microgravity limit at about 15 cm/s lies above or below that value.

sources.locator: as run matrix, rows 17, 47 and 61, columns AA and AD

answers.question: What did CFI find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: The CFI record (PSI-39) states objectives, not results: burning n-dodecane and n-dodecane/iso-dodecane droplets in the ISS Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus, the effect of helium dilution on cool flames, and how droplet size and pressure relate to flame extinction.
The record's objectives give pressures of 25.3 to 506.6 kPa, and its approach a gas mixture delivered to the chamber at 25.3 to 50.7 kPa.
The record dates CFI from 1 October 2020 to 20 October 2021 and lists 7 publications, an experimental table and 2,791 raw and 32 analysed data files.

From FLEX, not CFI: the 2015 ISS combustion guide reports that in spaceflight tests large alkane droplets in quiescent gas, after radiative loss put out their hot flame, kept vaporizing, supported by a cool flame that can burn for a prolonged time.

Describing an envisioned Cool Flames initiative that would use existing FLEX-2 hardware, the 2015 ISS combustion guide says reduced gravity has been shown to be particularly conducive to a low-temperature regime of very weak but persistent flames, invisible to the unaided eye, that will spontaneously re-ignite long after the visible flame has gone out.

inferred.text: Five of the seven publications the CFI record lists also appear in the FLEX record, among them the 2012 paper the 2015 guide cites for cool flames found in FLEX and FLEX-2 droplet tests, so the list alone does not show which results come from CFI's own tests.

other_side.note: no CFI results in the documents, so no evidence either way

lead.text: The documents hold no CFI results, such as measured cool-flame behaviour or extinction diameters of n-dodecane droplets.

answers.question: What did DAFT / DAFT-2 find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: The DAFT / DAFT-2 record states objectives: to show that a TSI P-Trak particle counter modified for microgravity works on the ISS and to compare it with a DustTrak control, lowering the risk for the SAME smoke experiment.

The record's hypotheses, not findings: the P-Trak was expected not to work in microgravity, through clogging or obscuring by isopropanol or over-counting from air flow inside its optics chamber; modified to recycle the isopropanol by capillary action, it was hypothesized to work normally.

In its research impacts, the record speaks of "the successful adaptation of the TSI P-Trak for microgravity", which "can inform the design of instruments for use in other challenging Earth environments"; this is the record's statement, and the record gives no measurement behind it.

The record's approach used Arizona Red Dust, aerosolized with GN2 and held in 15-liter Mylar bags, as the aerosol standard, and compared the modified P-Trak's on-orbit particle counts with a DustTrak designed for microgravity.
The record lists two publications, one experimental table, 12 analysed-data files and 3 reports; none of them is among these documents, so their results are not here.
A 2015 guide to ISS combustion science describes the Dust Aerosol measurement Feasibility Test as having examined the background aerosol particulate levels on the ISS.

inferred.text: The record presents DAFT as a particle-counter test on a dust standard and mentions no burn, so its data files would concern measuring aerosols in microgravity, not how a cabin material ignites or spreads flame.

other_side.note: no results in the documents, so no evidence either way

lead.text: The documents hold no DAFT / DAFT-2 results, such as how the modified P-Trak's counts in microgravity compared with the DustTrak's.

answer.not_covered: The documents give no number of DAFT runs and no oxygen, pressure or airflow for them.

answers.question: What did Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: The PSI-60 record describes a ground study, June 2019 to August 2022, that set out to derive temperature distributions and soot volume fractions from SPICE data in PSI by analysing over 1600 raw DSLR images with advanced soot models.

The record's approach combines image analysis and modelling: colour-ratio pyrometry on raw Nikon images for soot temperature, SPICE's absolute light calibration for soot volume fraction, and a coupled flow, species and soot model run for Yale and ACME burner configurations in normal gravity and microgravity.
The record lists one published paper, from 2022, and one metadata file, with no experimental table; the paper's results are not in these documents.

The record's hypothesis, not a reported result: microgravity would give longer, more diffuse flames with lower temperatures and more soot than normal gravity, and feeding measured temperature fields into the simulations would reduce the gaps between measured and predicted soot distributions.
The record states that, for space applications, the results support safer fire detection, suppression and cleaner combustion technologies for long-duration missions; it gives none of those results.

inferred.text: Its soot values would come from SPICE flame images and SPICE's light calibration, so they analyse flames SPICE already burned rather than adding new flight tests.

other_side.note: no results of this analysis in the documents, so no evidence either way

lead.text: The documents hold no results of the PSI-60 analysis of SPICE data: no derived soot temperatures, soot volume fractions or model-to-measurement comparisons.

answer.not_covered: No fuel, oxygen, pressure or flow is given for the SPICE flames it analysed.

answers.question: What did Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: The PSI-62 record describes a ground study, May 2019 to April 2021, that set out to develop and validate flamelet generated manifold modelling of concurrent flame spread in microgravity, benchmarked on the BASS and BASS-II experiments.

Its approach tested an unsteady form of the method on BASS geometries including PMMA flat sheets, spheres and rods and wax cylinders, and turned BASS and BASS-II images into 3-D soot and temperature fields by two-colour tomography for comparison.

The record lists four published papers, the first by Olson and Ferkul and three co-authored by the principal investigator, and one metadata file, with no experimental table; none of the four papers is among these documents.

The record's hypothesis, not a reported result: the unsteady method could accurately reproduce concurrent flame spread in microgravity, including the "Goldilocks" flammability zone reported by Olson and Ferkul, by coupling near-wall thermal, mass-transport and chemical processes with far-field flow dynamics.

A section of the BASS-II summary report with the same title as that Olson and Ferkul paper places the minimum of the BASS-II flammability boundary for PMMA rods on ISS at about 13.5% final O2 and a stretch rate of 8 to 12 s–1, a weak-flow "Goldilocks" zone it calls typical of spacecraft ventilation near surfaces.

inferred.text: Given the shared title, the "Goldilocks" zone the model was to reproduce is most likely the weak-flow zone at the minimum of this BASS-II PMMA-rod boundary; any limit the model gives would be a prediction, and no document shows how close it came.

other_side.note: no results of this modelling in the documents, so no evidence either way

lead.text: The documents hold no results of the PSI-62 modelling: no predicted flame geometry, spread rates or flammability limits, and no comparison with BASS images.

answer.not_covered: No oxygen, pressure or flow value is given for any modelled case.

answers.question: What did FLEX-2 find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: The FLEX-2 record (PSI-68) states aims, not results: extend FLEX-1 to fuels and conditions that mimic real combustors and give benchmark data on bi-component droplet burning in ISS microgravity, to validate simulations and develop new theory.

The record's approach says chamber pressure was varied from 50.7 to 304.0 kPa and oxygen from 10 to 40% O2, diluent the balance, with chamber pressure and temperature recorded in near real time during ISS tests.

The 2015 ISS combustion guide credits FLEX and FLEX-2 together, without separating them, with identifying radiative and diffusive extinction limits for heptane and methanol droplets in microgravity and a limiting oxygen index significantly lower than in normal gravity.

The 2015 ISS combustion guide's one FLEX-2 image is captioned as a comparison of sooting propensity in different diluents, for ethanol droplets burning in 30% O2 at 243.2 kPa; the caption gives no measured value.

The record lists the independently varied parameters as fuel type, ambient gas composition, ambient pressure, initial droplet diameter, droplet translation velocity and acceleration, and droplet spacing and initial size in a binary linear array.

inferred.text: Of the 48 publication titles in the FLEX-2 record, 36 also appear word for word in the FLEX record's list, so the record alone does not show which published results come from FLEX-2 tests.

other_side.note: no results reported for FLEX-2 alone, so no evidence either way

lead.text: The documents hold no results reported for FLEX-2 alone, such as its own measured extinction limits.

answer.not_covered: The documents give no list of FLEX-2 tests with their fuel, oxygen and pressure.

answers.question: What did FLEX find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: A 2011 FLEX paper on 2 to 4 mm methanol droplets in quiescent microgravity aboard the ISS reports ignition and some burning at 13% O2, nitrogen the balance, and 101.3 kPa.

The 2015 ISS combustion guide says FLEX had shown the flammability limit of its heptane and methanol droplets is lower in reduced gravity, implying terrestrial inert-gas suppressant standards lack the same margin of safety there.

On the ISS at 101.3 kPa, the authors class methanol droplets at 14% O2 or less as radiative extinctions, likely transient burns whose extinction diameter likely depends on ignition energy, so, in a sense, such conditions might be considered outside the limiting oxygen index.

In the 2011 FLEX paper, of over two hundred methanol and heptane droplet burns on the ISS in oxygen/nitrogen/CO2 mixtures by then, 104 were methanol, and it examines only the 54 that gave an extinction diameter with the droplet in the back-lit camera's view.

For single large alkane droplets burning in quiescent gas in FLEX spaceflight tests, the 2015 ISS combustion guide reports that after radiative loss put out the hot flame, a cool flame kept the droplet vaporizing and can burn for a prolonged time.

inferred.text: These FLEX results concern liquid methanol and alkane droplets in quiescent microgravity, so they do not by themselves give the oxygen limit of any solid cabin material.

other_side.note: the authors suggest the burns at 14% O2 or less might be considered outside the limiting oxygen index, against the 13% O2 ignition

lead.text: On the ISS, methanol droplets at 101.3 kPa ignited with some burning at 13% O2 in nitrogen; the authors suggest such conditions might be considered outside the limiting oxygen index.

answer.not_covered: The documents give no normal-gravity oxygen limit for methanol droplets.

answers.question: What did SAFFIRE-I find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: In microgravity on an unoccupied ISS resupply vehicle, a 40.6 by 94 cm sheet of 0.37 mm SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric burned in air in 20 cm/s concurrent flow at an average spread rate of 1.8 mm/s.
The SIBAL fabric burned for the 420 s allotted and went out immediately when the air flow was shut off (microgravity, unoccupied ISS resupply vehicle, 20 cm/s concurrent flow before the shut-off).

The 2017 Saffire deck concludes that, unlike in 1 g, a steady flame was achieved even on Saffire I's wide sample in concurrent flow, its length reaching a plateau of around 40 mm; its results table gives the fabric's 1-g spread as acceleratory, with no 1-g test conditions printed.

Only the concurrent test was planned; a contingency opposed-flow test on the roughly 10% of fabric left burned for 70 s in 20 cm/s flow at an average 1.3 mm/s, with a 24 mm long flame (microgravity, about 21.5% O2 by the deck's CO2-based estimate).

Reports differ on Saffire I's atmosphere: initial 21.7% O2 by ISS reading in the 2017 deck, its oxygen chart starting near 22.6; 21% and 100 kPa in a 2021 paper; 21.7% and 102 kPa at hatch closing in a 2022 paper.
A 2022 paper on Saffire I to V and two BASS tests finds concurrent spread rates and flame lengths over thin fabrics in microgravity strongly affected by duct size, even in ducts over 30 cm tall.

inferred.text: Saffire I burned one material in one vehicle atmosphere, so it reports how SIBAL spreads and responds to a flow shut-off in that atmosphere, not the low-g flammability limits the PSI record lists among its objectives.

other_side.note: the flame went out at once when the air flow was shut off, set against 420 s of burning in 20 cm/s flow

lead.text: In microgravity, Saffire I's large SIBAL fabric burned for 420 s in 20 cm/s concurrent flow and went out at once when the flow stopped; one sample, no repeats.

answer.not_covered: No Saffire I test at another oxygen level or pressure.

answers.question: What did SAFFIRE-II find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: In microgravity in 20 cm/s flow (three concurrent, one opposed), no flame spread on any of four silicone sheets 0.27 to 1.03 mm thick: after igniter shut-off, a tiny flame remained and quickly went out.

In upward 1-g tests, conditions not printed, 0.27 mm silicone sheets were almost always completely consumed and 1.03 mm sheets would not burn; the 2017 deck concludes that silicone's flammability appears reduced in microgravity, at least at the flow speeds tested.
In microgravity, the two 5 cm wide, 0.37 mm SIBAL fabric samples burned their full length, spreading at 2.1 mm/s in 20 cm/s and 2.6 mm/s in 25 cm/s concurrent flow.

On composite sample 2-7, the thin PMMA sheet forming its first 5 cm burned away in about two minutes, its flame heating the base of the Nomex HT90-40 fabric beyond, yet the fabric was not ignited (microgravity, 20 cm/s concurrent flow).

Two PMMA slabs of nominal 1 cm thickness, lit by 97 W igniters left on for 30 s, burned for 600 and 900 s with flames anchored at the sample base and a very slow regression of 0.01 to 0.04 mm/s (microgravity, 20 cm/s concurrent flow).

Using Saffire II data for sample 9, a 10 mm PMMA slab in air at 20 cm/s and atmospheric pressure, a 2018 paper finds its microgravity spread rate from flame-tip progress, about 0.09 mm/s read from a figure, significantly lower than in 1-g tests of 10 mm PMMA at 100 kPa and 20 cm/s upward air flow.

Reports differ on Saffire II's atmosphere: initial 22.1% O2 (ISS reading) in the 2017 deck, about 21.5% read from its oxygen chart; 21% and 100 kPa for the fabric samples in a 2021 paper; 22.1% and 103 kPa at hatch closing in a 2022 paper.
Each of the nine samples was a single test, at 20 cm/s except one SIBAL sample at 25 cm/s in the 2017 deck; the PSI record gives the flow as 20 or 30 cm/s depending on the sample material.

inferred.text: All nine samples were tested in one vehicle atmosphere, printed between 21% and 22.1% O2, so Saffire II reports outcomes at that oxygen rather than the low-gravity oxygen flammability limits the 2017 deck names as Saffire 2's objective.

Sample 2-7 ran at about 21.5% to 22.1% O2 by the 2017 deck's figures, below the O2 of around 24 to 25% the deck cites for Nomex HT90-40 to burn on Earth, so its non-ignition in microgravity agrees with that Earth figure.

other_side.note: the two SIBAL fabric samples burned their full length, set against silicone sheets with no flame spread and Nomex that was not ignited

lead.text: In microgravity, Saffire II's SIBAL fabric and PMMA burned; four silicone sheets kept only a brief, non-spreading flame and Nomex HT90-40 was not ignited; each sample ran once.

answer.not_covered: No Saffire II test at another oxygen level or pressure.

answers.question: What did Parabolic flight tests (partial gravity) find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: The 2026 deck, citing Sacksteder's KC-135 experiments, states downward flame spread rate peaks in partial gravity; its plot reads about 0.84 to 0.89 cm/s near 0.37 g against about 0.74 to 0.81 cm/s near 1 g (material, oxygen and pressure not stated).
Upward spread on the same plot was about 3.1 to 3.7 cm/s near 0.31 to 0.38 g and about 1.0 to 1.3 cm/s near 0.1 g (read from a figure).
In a lunar-gravity (0.165 g) parabolic-flight test, Day 2 parabola 29, a 5-cm-wide SIBAL fabric strip in 21% O2 at 101.3 kPa spread steadily downward for the entire 20-s test.

The deck gives a downward flame-base spread rate in air of 0.086 cm/s for a SIBAL lunar-gravity aircraft test and 0.11 cm/s for a SIBAL lunar-gravity drop test with centrifuge (pressure and sample width not stated).
In the deck's lunar-gravity aircraft test of SIBAL (Test 2-29), the plotted g-level started near 0.26 g, then stayed between about 0.14 and 0.19 g until about 25 s (read from a figure).
The deck states that drop towers and aircraft are limited by duration and/or Coriolis-force effects.

inferred.text: Test 2-29's printed flame-base fit, Vf = 0.86t + 35.2 with position in mm and time in s, gives 0.86 mm/s, the same as the 0.086 cm/s quoted for the SIBAL lunar-gravity aircraft test, so that rate most likely comes from Test 2-29.

A deck caption on 2.2-cm SIBAL says downward spread cannot be achieved on Earth, so the steady downward spread of 5-cm SIBAL at lunar gravity in 21% O2 and 101.3 kPa shows, in one aircraft test, a spread direction that lunar gravity allowed for this fabric.

other_side.note: upward spread slowing as gravity fell, against downward spread peaking in partial gravity

lead.text: In KC-135 experiments the 2026 deck cites, downward flame spread peaked in partial gravity and upward spread slowed as gravity fell; material, oxygen and pressure are not given.

answer.not_covered: No flammability limit from a lunar- or Martian-gravity aircraft test.

answers.question: What did Centrifuge drop tests (partial gravity) find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: OVR-04 Table I puts the Martian- and lunar-gravity oxygen limits of Mylar G and Ultem 1000 films at 70.3 kPa and Nomex HT90-40 fabric at 101.3 kPa below their 1-g limits; the lunar values are earlier data it cites.

Below lunar gravity the Mylar G limits rose again: about 19% O2 at about 0.07 and 0.1 g in two added points (read from a figure; pressure not stated), against 14.1% and 15.6% at lunar gravity and 70.3 kPa.

In a 2024 study the 2026 deck cites, upward-burning ¼-inch PMMA rods ignited in 1 g by a retractable hot wire gave a centrifuge-drop extinction boundary that dips to about 13.7% O2 near 0.16 to 0.2 g, below about 14.75% at 1 g (read from a slide figure; pressure and test flow not stated).

At Martian gravity (0.38 g) in concurrent flow, a 5-mil Mylar G film flame, lit with a tissue-strip assist, survived the whole 5.18 s drop at 18% O2 and 70.3 kPa; in another test at 17% O2 it went out.

On a drop-bus rig with a turntable platform, 2-cm-wide SIBAL fabric burned both upward and downward at lunar gravity (0.165 g) in air at 101.3 kPa; the deck gives 0.11 cm/s for the downward flame-base spread in air of a lunar-gravity centrifuge drop test of SIBAL.
The 2026 deck notes a drop tower limits a test to about 5 s: maybe long enough for the gas phase to respond, typically too short for the solid.

OVR-04 takes as its low-gravity limits the lowest oxygen at which a flame survived the full drop and the highest at which it went out during the drop, and notes these differ from the 1-g criteria because of drop-time limits.

At their Martian survival limits (Nomex HT90-40 at 19.9% O2 and 101.3 kPa, Ultem 1000 at 22.0% and 70.3 kPa) the flames were dim, under 1 cm long and shrinking as the drop ended; the authors judge it likely they might have gone out with more time and call the limits found conservative.

inferred.text: In the Martian drops the igniter was switched on 1 s (Mylar G) or 2.1 s (Ultem 1000, Nomex HT90-40) before release and ran 2 s or 3.5 s in all, so it was still on for about the first 1 to 1.4 s of each 5.18 s drop.

The lowest limits sit at lunar gravity for Mylar G and Ultem 1000 at 70.3 kPa and near 0.16 to 0.2 g for the PMMA rods, but at Martian gravity for Nomex HT90-40 at 101.3 kPa, so in these tests the gravity level giving the lowest limit differs by material.

other_side.note: Mylar G limits back near 19% O2 below lunar gravity, against the low lunar and Martian limits

lead.text: In centrifuge drops, three sheet materials burned below their 1-g oxygen limits at lunar and Martian gravity, Mylar G less so below lunar gravity; each drop lasted about 5 s.

answer.not_covered: No centrifuge test printed above 22% O2 or below 70 kPa.

answers.question: What did Confined Combustion (ISS) find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: On the ISS at about 22% O2, 101 kPa and 7 cm/s, SIBAL fabric between parallel baffles had its fastest spread and longest flame at 4.0 cm spacing for all three baffle types.
On the ISS at about 22% O2, 101 kPa and 7 cm/s, SOF-08 states that at about 1 cm spacing, for every baffle type, the flame failed to ignite or went out before the sample end.

Preflight, at 7 cm/s imposed, flow between the baffles fell about 28% from 5 to 3 cm spacing; SOF-08 states the flow entering between the baffles may be below the imposed value, especially when they are close.

At 4.0 cm spacing on the ISS at about 22% O2, 101 kPa and 7 cm/s, SIBAL spread at about 2.15 mm/s between polished aluminum baffles, 1.95 between black and 1.74 between transparent ones (read from a figure); SOF-08 attributes the faster spread to radiation the polished baffles reflect back.

sources.locator: Fig. 7; C. Effects of Radiation Feedback

data.text: In all tests, pressure and oxygen in the ISS glovebox stayed at ambient values, 101 kPa and about 22% O2, with oxygen varying from 21.3% to 22.9% from day to day.

On the ISS at about 22% O2 and 101 kPa, SIBAL flames kept growing through the test above 15 cm/s imposed flow except at small spacing, which SOF-08 says might be specific to the tested sample length, and SOF-08 focuses on the cases that reached a steady state.

SOF-08 reports that earlier BASS tests of the same SIBAL at 101 kPa, 21% O2 and 5 cm/s spread about 42% faster than its no-baffle case on the ISS at about 22% O2 and 7 cm/s, and names its wider sample card, 6.1 against 3.6 cm, as one possible cause.

inferred.text: SOF-08 mentions no repeated burn, and its profile figures overlay one test per condition: five tests from 2.0 cm black-baffle spacing to no baffles, and three baffle types at 4.0 cm; so each spacing and baffle type appears to rest on a single burn.

SOF-08 reports spread rates and flame lengths of its own tests only at about 22% O2, 101 kPa and 5 or 7 cm/s on the ISS, so these documents do not show where the 4.0 cm optimum or the 1 cm failure would fall at other oxygen levels, pressures or faster flows.

other_side.note: No ignition or early extinction at about 1 cm spacing, set against steady spread from 2.0 cm spacing to no baffles

lead.text: For SIBAL on the ISS at about 22% O2 and 7 cm/s, flames spread fastest with baffles 4 cm apart but failed at 1 cm; oxygen stayed at ISS ambient.

answer.not_covered: No Confined Combustion results for the 1 mm PMMA slabs it also tested.

answers.question: What did Drop tower tests (NASA Glenn) find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: This group's drop-tower rows come from OVR-03 (Nomex HT90-40 fabric, Ultem 1000 and Mylar G film flammability tests and Kimwipes spread tests; OVR-04 lists the same 0g limit values) and BAS-01 and BAS-04 (cast PMMA rod blowoff drops); two SIBAL fabric images from OVR-13 are filed here too, though the slide names no platform.
Mylar G at 70.3 kPa burned through a 5.18 s drop at 17% O2 and 30 cm/s concurrent flow; OVR-03 puts its 1-g Test 1 MOC at 20% O2, from WSTF data.

OVR-04 finds the 0g margin (30 cm/s concurrent) of charring Ultem 1000 at 70.3 kPa and Nomex HT90-40 at 101.4 kPa very close to zero relative to hot-wire-ignited WSTF Test 1 limits; OVR-03 calls Ultem's significantly negative.
In OVR-03 limit tests, flames lit in 1 g in richer oxygen had about 5 s in test gas; the authors note some may have gone out later, calling the limits a conservative 0g measure.

In 10 mil Ultem 1000 film drops at 70.3 kPa and about 30 cm/s concurrent flow, flames both burned and went out at about 22% and about 23% O2 (read from a figure); the caption attributes such different results near the boundary to the randomness of the flames and sample curling, which affects the airflow.

OVR-03 observed the minimum of Ultem 1000's 0g flammability curve (70.3 kPa) in concurrent flow at 30 cm/s, the highest velocity the drop rig could reach, so Nomex HT90-40 and Mylar G were tested at 30 cm/s concurrent, which it cites as a reasonable maximum local spacecraft ventilation velocity.

BAS-01 and BAS-04 report that cast PMMA rod blowoff limits from 5.18 s drops, at about 14% to 16% final O2 (read from figures; pressure not printed), agree very well with the BASS-II blowoff limits measured on the ISS; BAS-04 takes this to imply that rod preheat levels do not affect blowoff extinction.

BAS-01 states the 5.18 s PMMA rod drops could show blowoff extinction, whose characteristic time was less than the drop time, but not quenching extinction at very low forced flow, whose characteristic time was substantially longer.

OVR-03's Kimwipes correlations, developed with 30 concurrent and 10 opposed drop tests at 24.8 to 101.4 kPa, predict faster opposed than concurrent spread over virtually all spacecraft atmospheres and flows, with similar rates at 20 to 25% O2; the authors find it plausible that the 0g limits, taken mostly in concurrent flow, may also differ in opposed flow.

inferred.text: The 1-g MOC needs at least five passing samples, while the drop limits use slightly modified definitions that OVR-04 links to the number of drops otherwise needed, and OVR-03 reports no drop count, so each 0g limit may rest on few drops.
Nomex HT90-40 and Mylar G 0g limits come from one flow, 30 cm/s concurrent, so these documents hold no 0g limit for them at the 5 to 20 cm/s that OVR-03 cites as nominal spacecraft ventilation.

other_side.note: near-zero 0g margins for Ultem and Nomex in OVR-04, set against Mylar G burning below its 1-g limits

lead.text: In 5.18 s microgravity drops, Mylar G burned at oxygen below its 1-g Test 1 limits, Ultem and Nomex near theirs in one paper; flames had about 5 s.

answer.not_covered: No limit test in these drops above about 26% O2.

answers.question: What did FLARE ground tests (1-g) find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: In 1 g, the limiting oxygen of all four wires rose as forced opposed flow went from 4 to 100 cm/s: for LDPE on copper, from about 16.4% to about 19.8% O2, read from a figure.

In 1 g at 40 to 100 cm/s opposed flow, copper-core wires had lower limiting oxygen than nickel-chrome ones for both insulations; the authors report the reverse at low flow in microgravity, partly from an earlier study's data.
Each 1-g limit came from the up-and-down method, which finds it in a small number of tests; a test counted as flammable if the flame spread past a line 60 mm from the bottom of the holder.

In the 1-g oxygen index test at 4 cm/s forced flow, both ETFE wires gave about 36% O2 and both LDPE wires less than the oxygen level of air, read from a figure; the authors chose insulations with oxygen index below and above air on purpose.

The 1-g oxygen index tests ran at 4 cm/s forced flow, but the authors plot their limits at an assumed buoyant flow of 35 cm/s; the high-velocity limits are plotted at the forced flow, which the method defines by hot-wire anemometer, not bulk velocity.

The authors find the 1-g and microgravity limits well connected for every wire, so the 1-g oxygen index and high-velocity values tell whether the limit falls or rises further in microgravity; a quantitative minimum-limit prediction is left to future work.
FLR-05 gives the 1-g limits only as figure markers, with no table of values, and prints no test pressure or ambient temperature.

inferred.text: These 1-g limits come from one wire size, a 0.5 mm core and 0.8 mm outer diameter, with no pressure stated, so they do not show how thicker insulation or lower pressure would shift them.

other_side.note: copper cores below nickel-chrome at high flow in 1 g, the reverse of the order the authors report at low flow in microgravity

lead.text: In 1 g, each wire's oxygen limit rose from 4 to 100 cm/s forced flow; copper cores sat below nickel-chrome at high flow, opposite to low-flow microgravity; no pressure printed.

answer.not_covered: No lunar or Martian gravity test of these wires.

answers.question: What did Other 1-g tests find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: In SAF-04's upward 1-g tests, Saffire II silicone 0.27 mm thick was almost always fully consumed, 0.61 mm burned on average 7.6 of 30 cm, and 1.03 mm would not burn; oxygen and pressure not printed.

In microgravity at 20 cm/s concurrent or opposed flow, no Saffire II silicone sample, 0.27 to 1.03 mm thick, spread a flame: a tiny flame left when the igniter went off quickly went out; SAF-04 calls this surprising, since the 0.27 mm sample was entirely consumed in 1-g.
In BAS-09's 1-g tests, upward forced-flow blowoff limits of cast PMMA rods, radii 0.318 to 1.905 cm, were about 3 to 7 cm/s at 15% O2, rising roughly linearly with oxygen (read from a figure).

BAS-09 ran over 280 experiments, repeating each bracketing flow at least once, with oxygen from premixed bottles and pressure not printed; it discarded its 14% O2 tube data after a rod blew off at 14% O2, 2 cm/s and 1 g in repeated tests in a larger wind tunnel.

In centrifuge drop tests that OVR-13 reproduces from Olson and co-authors, upward-burning ¼-inch PMMA rods at a simulated 1 g burned steadily at about 15.1% O2 and went out at about 14.8% and 14.4%, read from a figure, pressure not printed; OVR-13 notes each drop lasts about 5 s, typically too short for the solid's response.

sources.locator: Flammability Boundary for upward-burning PMMA rods in centrifuge

data.text: OVR-04's table gives Nomex HT90-40 at 101.3 kPa a 1-g MOC of 22.1% O2 (Test 1 with a hot wire igniter) and a lunar-gravity drop-test MOC of 19.9%, under different limit criteria.

In SAF-09, 10 mm cast PMMA slabs burning upward in 1-g air at 20 cm/s forced flow spread (pyrolysis front) at about 0.92 mm/s at 100 kPa and about 0.27 mm/s at 40 kPa, three to five repeats each, read from a figure; the authors report the microgravity rate at 100 kPa significantly lower.

BAS-07 reports that SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric self-extinguishes when burning downward (opposed flow) in 1-g normal air, while in microgravity a 2 cm wide sample spread steadily against a 10 cm/s opposed flow until it ran out of fuel.

sources.locator: Comparison of 0-g and 1-g Opposed Flow Flames

inferred.text: Across SAF-04, SAF-09, BAS-07 and OVR-04, 1-g results miss low-gravity behaviour in both directions: silicone spread no flame and PMMA spread more slowly in microgravity at 20 cm/s, while SIBAL spread against the flow in microgravity and Nomex HT90-40 had lower oxygen limits in lunar gravity, under different limit criteria.

sources.locator: Comparison of 0-g and 1-g Opposed Flow Flames

inferred.text: The 1-g PMMA rod results near 14% to 15% O2 come from a quartz tube with forced flow, a larger wind tunnel and centrifuge drops, so they do not form a single 1-g limit for PMMA rods.

sources.locator: Flammability Boundary for upward-burning PMMA rods in centrifuge

other_side.note: 1.03 mm silicone that would not burn in 1-g, set against thinner samples that burned

lead.text: In SAF-04's upward 1-g tests, 0.27 mm silicone was almost always fully consumed and 1.03 mm would not burn; in microgravity at 20 cm/s, no silicone sample spread a flame.

answer.not_covered: None of these 1-g tests or limits is printed above 23.5% O2.

answers.question: What did NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 results (1-g) find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: CAB-03 reports a PTFE woven fabric that passed 1-g Test 1 alone at 36% O2 and 56.5 kPa, but failed layered on cotton at 36% O2 and 56.5 kPa, and at 34% and 32% O2 (pressure not printed).

At 37% O2 and 56.5 kPa, CAB-03 reports 1-g Test 1 passes for a para-aramid, meta-aramid and antistatic blend crew clothing fabric, alone and with a zipper sewn with PTFE thread, and for custom polyimide felt and meta-aramid patches sewn to the outer jacket fabric; treated Pellon polyester and polyurethane patches did not pass.
A 100% PBI 1x1 rib knit fabric passed 1-g MOC testing at 48% O2 and 56.5 kPa; CAB-03 prints no MOC value for it.

CAB-03 does not say whether its textile results used bottom-edge ignition or the J-configuration that avoids igniting the edge, and it calls edge ignition possibly unrealistically severe for textiles whose raw edges are not exposed in use.
In a 1-g Test 1 table that OVR-13 reproduces from a 2017 study, 15 to 30 cm samples of Solimide TA-301, Ultem, Nomex HT 90-40 and NX2245 had MOCs of 23.0% to 25.1% O2 at 70.3 kPa.

In OVR-13's Test 1 table at 70.3 kPa, unhemmed Nomex HT 90-40 had an MOC of 24.1% O2 with 15 cm samples and 23.1% with 30 cm samples, while the MOCs of Solimide TA-301 and Ultem stayed at 23.0% to 23.1% and of NX2245 at 25.0% to 25.1% across their lengths.

answers.question: What did White Sands Test Facility limits (1-g) find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: In WSTF's 1-g upward tests in initially quiescent gas at 101.3 kPa, half-inch-wide strips of 0.064-inch epoxy/glass had an MOC of 16% O2, standard 2.5-inch-wide samples 23%; PET film showed no such drop.

For SSP-M823 silicone elastomer (MQ) in 1-g upward tests in initially quiescent gas at 101.3 kPa, the MOC fell from 22% O2 at 0.040 inch to 17% at 0.004 inch; it is the only material in the thickness table, whose footnote says additional materials are being tested.
In initially quiescent gas at 101.3 kPa, exposing an edge raised the 1-g MOC of 0.061-inch PVC sheet from 35% to 39% O2, a result the authors call somewhat surprising and needing confirmation.

A 2008 report finds WSTF's published 1-g Test 1 MOCs generally not a strong function of pressure; the few exceptions appear to have halogens in common, Kel-F 81 rising from about 53% O2 at about 101 kPa to about 76% at about 48 kPa, read from its figure.

At 70.3 kPa, two reports put Mylar G's microgravity limits from 5.18-second drops at 30 cm/s concurrent flow about 4% O2 below WSTF's 1-g PET limits, and Ultem 1000's below in one report, not in the other; some drop flames may extinguish given longer time.

In the parametric-effects paper each value is a limit, not one test: oxygen was stepped 1% by volume in a closed 1400-litre chamber; at the MOC all samples, at least five, passed the burn-length criterion, and the ULOI, from the up-and-down method, is where extinguishing is about 50% likely.

sources.locator: I. Introduction; II. Experimental Apparatus and Procedures

inferred.text: The thickness effect rests on one silicone and the width effect on two materials besides PET film, with several table cells marked testing in progress, so the paper's tables do not show how far these set-up effects carry to other materials.
Of the 129 limits, 97 are at 101.3 kPa and none is below about 48 kPa; the seven near 48 kPa, one per material, are read from one figure that gives no sample forms.

other_side.note: an exposed edge raised PVC sheet's MOC, set against narrower and thinner samples that lowered limits

lead.text: WSTF's 1-g tests gave narrower epoxy/glass and thinner silicone lower oxygen limits, an exposed edge raised PVC sheet's MOC; in microgravity drops Mylar G burned below WSTF's 1-g PET limits.

answers.question: What did FLARE parabolic flights find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: The authors find all wires tested more flammable in microgravity than in 1 g: each one's limiting oxygen tended to fall as opposed flow fell over the flows tested, down to 5 cm/s in flight.

In flight at 0.01 g and 5 cm/s opposed flow, ETFE on a nickel-chrome core spread steadily at 23% O2; the authors find ETFE, flame resistant on the ground, has very low limits at low flow in microgravity.

Takahashi and colleagues' 2013 microgravity limits for LDPE on copper, about 17.5% and 18.1% O2 at about 14.5 and 19.2 cm/s, read from a figure, sit above FLR-05's flight limits; FLR-05 attributes this to weaker ignition energy.

Each parabola gave about 20 s at 0.01 g; citing earlier work that found residual gravity can generate about 3 cm/s of natural convection even on small flat sheets, the flights used constant forced opposed flows of 5 to 20 cm/s, from ignition on.

FLR-05 replots earlier microgravity limits by Takahashi and colleagues (2013) for LDPE wires and by Mizutani and colleagues (2018) for ETFE on copper, without stating on which platform they were run; for LDPE on nickel-chrome these are the only microgravity limits, FLR-05 having no flight data for it.
At 5 cm/s opposed flow in flight at 0.01 g, ETFE on copper spread at oxygen levels from about 28% to 41% O2, read from a figure.

inferred.text: Because the limits were still falling at 5 cm/s, the lowest flight flow, the minimum limit of these wires in microgravity may lie at a lower flow and a lower oxygen than any flight value.

other_side.note: an earlier study's LDPE-on-copper microgravity limits sit above FLR-05's flight limits, which FLR-05 attributes to weaker ignition

lead.text: All wires tested were more flammable in microgravity than 1 g, the authors find; some earlier LDPE-copper limits sat above theirs; each parabola gave about 20 s of microgravity.

answer.not_covered: FLR-05 prints no pressure for any microgravity test.

answers.question: What did ISS experiments reported by Zhao et al. find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: On the ISS, 2.2-cm-wide SIBAL fabric flames in concurrent flow quenched at about 18.7% O2 and 2.0 cm/s and at about 16.9% O2 and 2.8 cm/s, the quench flow rising as oxygen fell (read from a slide figure).
On the same plot, 2.2-cm SIBAL flames spread just above the quenching boundary down to about 16.9% O2 at about 3.7 cm/s, and at about 17.4% O2 and 5 cm/s (read from a figure).
A 2.2-cm sample at about 16.8% O2 and 3.7 cm/s is plotted as not ignited, as are two at about 16.4% O2 and 5 and 10 cm/s (read from a figure).
For 1.2-cm-wide samples at about 17.1 to 17.2% O2, the plot shows spread at about 10.5 to 26 cm/s, quenching at about 3 and 5 cm/s and blowoff at about 31 cm/s (read from a figure).
The slide cites its plot from Zhao and co-authors' 2017 paper and prints no pressure, ignition method or test duration; it shows four 2.2-cm quench points.

BAS-05, Zhao and co-authors' 2015 paper on the BASS and BASS-II SIBAL tests on the ISS at 101.3 kPa, found quenching by lowering the flow during some tests and reports six BASS-II quenching cases, four on 2.2-cm samples.

BAS-05 adds that very near the boundary ignition of the sample is sporadic, and that lowering the flow cannot fix the boundary's lowest-oxygen part accurately; it calls for a procedure with gradually decreasing oxygen.

inferred.text: The slide's plot carries the same six experimental series as the BASS-II flammability map in BAS-05, with markers at matching positions, so its points are most likely the BASS-II tests BAS-05 describes; the slide does not say so.

Spread at about 16.9% O2 and a failed ignition at about 16.8%, both near 3.7 cm/s, put the lowest-oxygen edge for 2.2-cm SIBAL in concurrent flow near 17% O2 in these tests; BAS-05's note on sporadic ignition near the boundary leaves that edge loosely fixed.

other_side.note: flames spreading just above the boundary down to about 16.9% O2, against quenching at lower flow

answer.not_covered: No quenching test of this fabric at reduced pressure or in partial gravity.

answers.question: What did Saffire IV to VI (Cygnus) find, and how far can I trust it?

sources.locator: III. Results and Fire Impact on Habitability

data.text: SAF-02 finds NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 quite successful at identifying highly flammable materials, but states that a pass cannot be assumed to show a material will not burn under the tested conditions in low gravity, where it says thick-fuel flames do not grow or spread concurrently and instead depend on surface regression to move forward.

answers.question: What did SoFIE (ISS) find, and how far can I trust it?

data.text: In SOF-02's 35 extinction tests of 4-cm PMMA spheres on the ISS at 101 ± 5 kPa, flames survived to slightly below 14% O2 near 10 cm/s, which SOF-02 calls considerably lower than normal-gravity PMMA values in conventional flammability tables.
In three tests of 4-cm PMMA spheres on the ISS at 101 ± 5 kPa, flames quenched at about 20% O2 in slow flows of about 0.8 to 2.2 cm/s.
In two tests of 4-cm PMMA spheres on the ISS at 101 ± 5 kPa and about 4.8 cm/s, flames quenched at 16.01% and 14.21% O2; SOF-02 attributes the lower limit to more heat-up of the solid.

SOF-02 states the SoFIE-GEL campaign ran 54 tests on the ISS and determined sphere limits over 13% to 34% O2 and about 15 to 111 kPa, but it publishes limit data only for 35 tests at 101 ± 5 kPa; SOF-03's five cases list 104 to 108 kPa.

On the ISS, SOF-02 reads oxygen and flow at the duct entrance, upstream of the 4-cm PMMA sphere, with an estimated uncertainty of ±0.25%, and takes each limit as the oxygen and flow at the instant of extinction, reached by changing the flow or by oxygen depletion in the sealed chamber.

At higher flows, SOF-02 reports that on 4-cm PMMA spheres on the ISS at 101 ± 5 kPa the front flame blew off first, then a flame held in the wake went out later at lower oxygen, down to about 13.3% O2 at about 42 cm/s (read from a figure).
In SoFIE's still-air ISS tests at an initial 30% O2 that fell during each burn, flames over PMMA sheets 0.2 to 1 mm thick went out before the sample end at both 101.3 and 50.7 kPa.

inferred.text: SOF-03's five cases sit on SOF-02's extinction map at matching flow and oxygen, with matching heat-loss labels where both print one, and 1409B is named in both papers, so SOF-03 likely re-reports five of SOF-02's 35 tests rather than adding independent ones.

On the ISS, PMMA sheets 0.2 to 1 mm thick went out in still air from an initial 30% O2 at 50.7 and 101.3 kPa, while 4-cm spheres in about 10 cm/s forced flow at 101 ± 5 kPa burned to slightly below 14% O2, so oxygen alone did not decide whether PMMA kept burning.

other_side.note: Quenching at about 20% O2 in slow flow, set against burning to slightly below 14% O2 near 10 cm/s

lead.text: For 4-cm PMMA spheres on the ISS, flames survived to slightly below 14% O2 near 10 cm/s, slower flows quenched them at higher oxygen, and SOF-02 finds preheating shifts limits.

answer.not_covered: These documents report no SoFIE sphere extinction limit at reduced pressure.
